How Many Calories Does Exercise Actually Burn?

Fitness trackers and cardio machines often overestimate calorie burn. A realistic look at exercise calories and why “eating them back” backfires.

March 20, 2026 Updated September 14, 2026 · 2 min read

Part 2 of 7 in Movement, sleep and water

Less than you think: a brisk 30-minute walk is roughly 120–200 calories and a hard 30-minute run 300–400, which is a snack, not a meal. Cardio machines, fitness trackers and apps routinely overestimate burn, sometimes by large margins. Understanding the real numbers keeps you from accidentally eating back your entire workout.

The overestimation problem

In one well-known lab test, wrist-worn trackers were off on calorie burn by anywhere from about 20% to over 90%, and the errors were not small in either direction. Cardio machines are often generous too. The number is a rough guess based on averages, not a precise measurement of your body.

Realistic ballparks

Actual burn depends on your size, intensity and fitness, but for a rough sense: a 30-minute brisk walk might burn 120–200 calories, a hard 30-minute run 300–400, and a weights session less than people expect. That is less than many single snacks add up to.

Why “eating back” calories backfires

If your tracker says you burned 500 calories and you eat an extra 500 to “refuel,” you can erase your entire deficit — especially since the 500 was likely overstated. This is a common reason exercise on its own delivers less weight loss than people expect.

The better approach

  • Set your calorie target based on your overall activity level, and don’t add food for each workout. If your app adds exercise calories back into the day’s budget, treat that number as a rough bonus, not as food you have to eat.
  • Treat exercise as a bonus for health and muscle, not a license to eat more.
  • If you do eat back calories, count only a fraction (say half) to stay safe.

Because the burn side is so unreliable, the intake side is where control lives. A food log, however you keep it, is a firmer number than a calorie-burn estimate.

Key takeaways

  • Trackers and machines often overestimate calorie burn significantly.
  • Real burn is smaller than most people assume.
  • “Eating back” exercise calories can erase your deficit.
  • Control intake; treat exercise burn as a rough bonus.

This article is general information, not medical advice.
